entries.4a7f3348f49e83f23c29dc1138b1ce58b1c38121: <div sID="gen19279" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="46" osisID="Ezek.46" sID="Ezek.46"/> <div eID="gen19279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19280" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. Some further rules given both to the priests and to the people, relating to their worship, <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.1-Ezek.46.15">ver. 1-15</reference>. II. A law concerning the prince's disposal of his inheritance, <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.16-Ezek.46.18">ver. 16-18</reference>. III. A description of the places provided for the boiling of the sacrifices and the baking of the meat-offerings, <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.19-Ezek.46.24">ver. 19-24</reference>.
entries.cb5cf8a26da403c4206e6088aa15f91256b43bcd: <div eID="gen19280" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Rules Relating to Worship. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19281" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; The gate of the inner court that looketh toward the east shall be shut the six working days; but on the sabbath it shall be opened, and in the day of the new moon it shall be opened. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the prince shall enter by the way of the porch of <hi type="italic">that</hi> gate without, and shall stand by the post of the gate, and the priests shall prepare his burnt offering and his peace offerings, and he shall worship at the threshold of the gate: then he shall go forth; but the gate shall not be shut until the evening. <hi type="super">3</hi> Likewise the people of the land shall worship at the door of this gate before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the sabbaths and in the new moons. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the burnt offering that the prince shall offer unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the sabbath day <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> six lambs without blemish, and a ram without blemish. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the meat offering <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> an ephah for a ram, and the meat offering for the lambs as he shall be able to give, and an hin of oil to an ephah. <hi type="super">6</hi> And in the day of the new moon <hi type="italic">it shall be</hi> a young bullock without blemish, and six lambs, and a ram: they shall be without blemish. <hi type="super">7</hi> And he shall prepare a meat offering, an ephah for a bullock, and an ephah for a ram, and for the lambs according as his hand shall attain unto, and a hin of oil to an ephah. <hi type="super">8</hi> And when the prince shall enter, he shall go in by the way of the porch of <hi type="italic">that</hi> gate, and he shall go forth by the way thereof. <hi type="super">9</hi> But when the people of the land shall come before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the solemn feasts, he that entereth in by the way of the north gate to worship shall go out by the way of the south gate; and he that entereth by the way of the south gate shall go forth by the way of the north gate: he shall not return by the way of the gate whereby he came in, but shall go forth over against it. <hi type="super">10</hi> And the prince in the midst of them, when they go in, shall go in; and when they go forth, shall go forth. <hi type="super">11</hi> And in the feasts and in the solemnities the meat offering shall be an ephah to a bullock, and an ephah to a ram, and to the lambs as he is able to give, and a hin of oil to an ephah. <hi type="super">12</hi> Now when the prince shall prepare a voluntary burnt offering or peace offerings voluntarily unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">one</hi> shall then open him the gate that looketh toward the east, and he shall prepare his burnt offering and his peace offerings, as he did on the sabbath day: then he shall go forth; and after his going forth <hi type="italic">one</hi> shall shut the gate. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thou shalt daily prepare a burnt offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">of</hi> a lamb of the first year without blemish: thou shalt prepare it every morning. <hi type="super">14</hi> And thou shalt prepare a meat offering for it every morning, the sixth part of an ephah, and the third part of a hin of oil, to temper with the fine flour; a meat offering continually by a perpetual ordinance unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">15</hi> Thus shall they prepare the lamb, and the meat offering, and the oil, every morning <hi type="italic">for</hi> a continual burnt offering. <div eID="gen19281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19282" type="x-p"/> Whether the rules for public worship here laid down were designed to be observed, even in those things wherein they differed from the law of Moses, and were so observed under the second temple, is not certain; we find not in the history of that latter part of the Jewish church that they governed themselves in their worship by these ordinances, as one would think they should have done, but only by law of Moses, looking upon this <hi type="italic">then</hi> in the next age after as mystical, and not literal. We may observe, in these verses, <div eID="gen19282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19283" type="x-p"/> I. That the place of worship was fixed, and rules were given concerning that, both to prince and people. <div eID="gen19283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19284" type="x-p"/> 1. The east gate, which was kept shut at other times, was to be opened on the sabbath days, on the moons (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.1">v. 1</reference>), and whenever the prince offered a voluntary offering, <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.12">v. 12</reference>. Of the keeping of this gate ordinarily shut we read before (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.2">ch. xliv. 2</reference>); whereas the other gates of the court were opened every day, this was opened only on high days and on special occasions, when it was opened for the prince, who was to <hi type="italic">go in by the way of the porch of that gate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.2">v. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.8">8</reference>. Some think he went in with the priests and Levites into the <hi type="italic">inner court</hi> (for into that court this gate was the entrance), and they observe that magistrates and ministers should join forces, and go the same way, hand in hand, in promoting the service of God. But it should rather seem that he did not go <hi type="italic">through</hi> the gate (as the glory of the Lord had done), though it was open, but he went <hi type="italic">by the way of the porch of the gate,</hi> stood <hi type="italic">at the post of the gate,</hi> and <hi type="italic">worshipped at the threshold of the gate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.2">v. 2</reference>), where he had a full view of the priests' performances at the altar, and signified his concurrence in them, for himself and for the people of the land, that stood behind him <hi type="italic">at the door of that gate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.3">v. 3</reference>. Thus must every prince show himself to be of David's mind, who would very willingly be a <hi type="italic">door-keeper in the house of his God,</hi> and, as the word there is, <hi type="italic">lie at the threshold,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.84.10">Ps. lxxxiv. 10</reference>. Note, The greatest of men are less than the least of the ordinances of God. Even princes themselves, when they draw near to God, must worship <hi type="italic">with reverence and godly fear,</hi> owning that even they are unworthy to approach to him. But Christ is <hi type="italic">our prince,</hi> whom God causes to <hi type="italic">draw near</hi> and <hi type="italic">approach to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.30.21">Jer. xxx. 21</reference>. <div eID="gen19284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19285" type="x-p"/> 2. As to the north gate and south gate, by which they entered into the <hi type="italic">court of the people</hi> (not into the inner court), there was this rule given, that whoever came in at the <hi type="italic">north gate</hi> should go out at the <hi type="italic">south gate,</hi> and whoever came in at the <hi type="italic">south gate</hi> should go out at the <hi type="italic">north gate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.9">v. 9</reference>. Some think this was to prevent thrusting and jostling one another; for God is <hi type="italic">the God of order, and not of confusion.</hi> We may suppose that they came in at the gate that was next their own houses, but, when they went away, God would have them go out at that gate which would lead them <hi type="italic">the furthest way about,</hi> that they might have time for meditation; being thereby obliged to go a great way round the sanctuary, they might have an opportunity <hi type="italic">to consider the palaces</hi> of it, and, if they improved their time well in fetching this circuit, they would call it the nearest way home. Some observe that this may remind us, in the service of God, to be still pressing forward (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.13">Phil. iii. 13</reference>) and not to <hi type="italic">look back,</hi> and, in our attendance upon ordinances, not to go back as we came, but more holy, and heavenly, and spiritual. <div eID="gen19285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19286" type="x-p"/> 3. It is appointed that <hi type="italic">the people shall worship at the door of the east gate,</hi> where the prince does, he at the head and they attending him, both <hi type="italic">on the sabbath and on the new moons</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.3">v. 3</reference>), and that, when they come in and go out, the prince shall be <hi type="italic">in the midst of them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.10">v. 10</reference>. Note, Great men should, by their constant and reverent attendance on God in public worship, give a good example to their inferiors, both engaging them and encouraging them to do likewise. It is a very graceful becoming thing for persons of quality to go to church with their servants, and tenants, and poor neighbours about them, and to behave themselves there with an air of seriousness and devotion; and those who thus honour God with their honour he will delight to honour. <div eID="gen19286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19287" type="x-p"/> II. That the ordinances of worship were fixed. Though the prince is supposed himself to be a very hearty zealous friend to the sanctuary, yet it is not left to him, no, not in concert with the priests, to appoint what sacrifices shall be offered, but God himself appoints them; for it is his prerogative to institute the rites and ceremonies of religious worship. 1. Every morning, as duly as the morning came, they must offer <hi type="italic">a lamb</hi> for a <hi type="italic">burnt-offering,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.13">v. 13</reference>. It is strange that no mention is made of the evening sacrifice; but Christ having come, and having offered himself now <hi type="italic">in the end of the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.26">Heb. ix. 26</reference>), we are to look upon him as the evening sacrifice, about the time of the offering up of which he died. 2. On the sabbath days, whereas by the law of Moses four lambs were to be offered (<reference osisRef="Num.28.9">Num. xxviii. 9</reference>), it is here appointed that (at the prince's charge) there shall be <hi type="italic">six lambs</hi> offered, <hi type="italic">and a ram</hi> besides (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.4">v. 4</reference>), to intimate how much we should abound in sabbath work, now in gospel-time, and what plenty of the spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise we should offer up to God on that day; and, if <hi type="italic">with such sacrifice God is well-pleased,</hi> surely we have a great deal of reason to be so. 3. On the new moons, in the beginning of their months, there was over and above the usual sabbath-sacrifices the additional offering of a young bullock, <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.6">v. 6</reference>. Those who do much for God and their souls, statedly and constantly, must yet, upon some occasions, do still more. 4. All the sacrifices were to be <hi type="italic">without blemish;</hi> so Christ, the great sacrifice, was (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.19">1 Pet. i. 19</reference>), and so Christians, who are to present themselves to God as living sacrifices, should aim and endeavour to be—<hi type="italic">blameless, and harmless, and without rebuke.</hi> 5. All the sacrifices were to have their meat-offerings annexed to them, for so the law of Moses had appointed, to show what a good table God keeps in his house and that we ought to honour him with the fruit of our ground as well as with the fruit of our cattle, because in both he has blessed us, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.4">Deut. xxviii. 4</reference>. In the beginning, Cain offered the one and Abel the other. Some observe that the meat-offerings here are much larger in proportion than they were by the law of Moses. Then the proportion was <hi type="italic">three tenth-deals to a bullock,</hi> and <hi type="italic">two to a ram</hi> (so many tenth parts of an ephah) and half a hin of oil at the most (<reference osisRef="Num.15.6-Num.15.9">Num. xv. 6-9</reference>); but here, for every bullock and every ram, a whole ephah and a whole hin of oil (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.7">v. 7</reference>), which intimates that under the gospel, the great atoning sacrifice having been offered, these unbloody sacrifices shall be more abounded in; or, in general, it intimates that as now, under the gospel, God abounds in the gifts of his grace to us, more than under the law, so we should abound in the returns of praise and duty to him. But it is observable that in the meat-offering <hi type="italic">for the lambs</hi> the prince is allowed to offer <hi type="italic">as he shall be able to give</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.5-Ezek.46.6">v. 5, 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.11">11</reference>), <hi type="italic">as his hand shall attain unto.</hi> Note, Princess themselves must spend as they can afford; and even in that which is laid out in works of piety God expects and requires but that we should do according to our ability, every man <hi type="italic">as God has prepared him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.2">1 Cor. xvi. 2</reference>. God has not <hi type="italic">made us to serve with an offering</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.23">Isa. xliii. 23</reference>), but considers our frame and state. Yet this will not countenance those who pretend a disability that is not real, or those who by their extravagances in other things disable themselves to do the good they should. And we find those praised who, in an extraordinary case of charity, went not <hi type="italic">only to their power,</hi> but <hi type="italic">beyond their power.</hi>
entries.202bc1a5122a9918ed0ef3b46cf398c6e27c7608: <div eID="gen19287" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Laws Concerning the Prince's Inheritance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19288" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; If the prince give a gift unto any of his sons, the inheritance thereof shall be his sons'; it <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> their possession by inheritance. <hi type="super">17</hi> But if he give a gift of his inheritance to one of his servants, then it shall be his to the year of liberty; after it shall return to the prince: but his inheritance shall be his sons' for them. <hi type="super">18</hi> Moreover the prince shall not take of the people's inheritance by oppression, to thrust them out of their possession; <hi type="italic">but</hi> he shall give his sons inheritance out of his own possession: that my people be not scattered every man from his possession. <div eID="gen19288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19289" type="x-p"/> We have here a law for the limiting of the power of the prince in the disposing of the crown-lands. 1. If he have a <hi type="italic">son</hi> that is a favourite, or has merited well, he may, if he please, as a token of his favour and in recompence for his services, settle some parts of his lands upon him and his heirs for ever (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.16">v. 16</reference>), provided it do not go out of the family. There may be a cause for parents, when their children have grown up, to be more kind to one than to another, as Jacob gave to Joseph one portion <hi type="italic">above his brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.48.22">Gen. xlviii. 22</reference>. 2. Yet, if he have a servant that is a favourite, he may not in like manner settle lands upon him, <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.17">v. 17</reference>. The servant might have the rents, issues, and profits, for such a term, but the inheritance, the <hi type="italic">jus proprietarium—the right of proprietorship,</hi> shall remain in the prince and his heirs. It was fit that a difference should be put between a child and a servant, like that <reference osisRef="John.8.35">John viii. 35</reference>. <hi type="italic">The servant abides not in the house for ever,</hi> as the son does. 3. What estates he gives his children must be of his own (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.18">v. 18</reference>): He <hi type="italic">shall not take of the people's inheritance,</hi> under pretence of having many children to provide for; he shall not find ways to make them forfeit their estates, or to force them to sell them and so <hi type="italic">thrust his subjects out of their possession;</hi> but let him and his sons be content with their own. It is far from being a prince's honour to increase the wealth of his family and crown by encroaching upon the rights and properties of his subjects; nor will he himself be a gainer by it at last, for he will be but a poor prince when the people are <hi type="italic">scattered every man from his possession,</hi> when they quit their native country, being forced out of it by oppression, choosing rather to live among strangers that are free people, and where what they have they can call their own, be it ever so little. It is the interest of princes to rule in the hearts of their subjects, and then all they have is, in the best manner, at their service. It is better for themselves to gain their affections by protecting their rights than to gain their estates by invading them.
entries.00e90329915753743fc68c05a96c061e1760de98: <div eID="gen19289" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Buildings about the Temple. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19290" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> After he brought me through the entry, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> at the side of the gate, into the holy chambers of the priests, which looked toward the north: and, behold, there <hi type="italic">was</hi> a place on the two sides westward. <hi type="super">20</hi> Then said he unto me, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the place where the priests shall boil the trespass offering and the sin offering, where they shall bake the meat offering; that they bear <hi type="italic">them</hi> not out into the utter court, to sanctify the people. <hi type="super">21</hi> Then he brought me forth into the utter court, and caused me to pass by the four corners of the court; and, behold, in every corner of the court <hi type="italic">there was</hi> a court. <hi type="super">22</hi> In the four corners of the court <hi type="italic">there were</hi> courts joined of forty <hi type="italic">cubits</hi> long and thirty broad: these four corners <hi type="italic">were</hi> of one measure. <hi type="super">23</hi> And <hi type="italic">there was</hi> a row <hi type="italic">of building</hi> round about in them, round about them four, and <hi type="italic">it was</hi> made with boiling places under the rows round about. <hi type="super">24</hi> Then said he unto me, These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the places of them that boil, where the ministers of the house shall boil the sacrifice of the people. <div eID="gen19290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19291" type="x-p"/> We have here a further discovery of buildings about the temple, which we did not observe before, and those were places to boil the flesh of the offerings in, <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.20">v. 20</reference>. He that kept such a plentiful table at his altar needed large kitchens; and a wise builder will provide conveniences of that kind. Observe, 1. Where those boiling-places were situated. There were some at the entry into the inner court (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.19">v. 19</reference>) and others under the rows, in the four corners of the outer court, <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.21-Ezek.46.23">v. 21-23</reference>. These were the places where, it is likely, there was most room to spare for this purpose; and this purpose was found for the spare room, that none might be lost. It is a pity that holy ground should be waste ground. 2. What use they were put to. In those places they were to <hi type="italic">boil the trespass-offering and the sin-offering,</hi> those parts of them which were allotted to the priests and which were more sacred than the flesh of the peace-offerings, of which the offerer also had a share. There also they were to <hi type="italic">bake the meat-offering,</hi> their share of it, which they had from the altar for their own tables, <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.20">v. 20</reference>. Care was taken that they should not <hi type="italic">bear them out into the outer court, to sanctify the people.</hi> Let them not pretend to sanctify the people with this holy flesh, and so impose upon them; or let not the people imagine that by touching those sacred things they were sanctified, and made any the better or more acceptable to God. It should seem (from <reference osisRef="Hag.2.12">Hag. ii. 12</reference>) that there were those who had such a conceit; and therefore the priests must not carry any of the holy flesh away with them, lest they should encourage that conceit. Ministers must take heed of doing any thing to bolster up ignorant people in their superstitious vanities.  <chapter eID="Ezek.46"/> <div eID="gen19291" type="x-p"/>

entries.72bbe00045922b98c05fa36ed17d9ed87d5d0ac6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11890"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 46</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.46.1-Ezek.46.24">Eze 46:1-24</reference>. Continuation of the Ordinances for the Prince and for the People in Their Worship.</title> <div sID="gen21484" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11890"/>2. The prince is to go through the east gate without (open on the Sabbath only, to mark its peculiar sanctity) to the entrance of the gate of the inner court; he is to go no further, but "stand by the post" (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.14">1Ki 8:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.22">22</reference>, Solomon standing before the altar of the Lord in the presence of the congregation; also <reference osisRef="2Kgs.11.14">2Ki 11:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.3">23:3</reference>, "by a pillar": the customary place), the court within belonging exclusively to the priests. There, as representative of the people, in a peculiarly near relation to God, he is to present his offerings to Jehovah, while at a greater distance, the people are to stand worshipping at the outer gate of the same entrance. The offerings on Sabbaths are larger than those of the Mosaic law, to imply that the worship of God is to be conducted by the prince and people in a more munificent spirit of self-sacrificing liberality than formerly. <div eID="gen21484" type="x-p"/>
entries.83a9912b6af0054721ac722d64cd957c4f3d2eb4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11891"/><div sID="gen21485" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11891"/>9. The worshippers were on the great feasts to pass from one side to the other, through the temple courts, in order that, in such a throng as should attend the festivals, the ingress and egress should be the more unimpeded, those going out not being in the way of those coming in. <div eID="gen21485" type="x-p"/>
entries.07d36163a5b73ebed012105ec3728d433b1acb58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11892"/><div sID="gen21486" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11892"/><hi type="bold">10. prince in the midst--</hi>not isolated as at other times, but joining the great throng of worshippers, at their head, after the example of David (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.4">Psa 42:4</reference>, "I had gone with the multitude ... to the house of God, with the voice of joy and praise, with a multitude that kept holy day"); the highest in rank animating the devotions of the rest by his presence and example. <div eID="gen21486" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f17a261df31ee4f3d34e9e31f5323856447e8d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11893"/><div sID="gen21487" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11893"/>12-15. Not only is he to perform official acts of worship on holy days and feasts, but in "voluntary" offerings daily he is to show his individual zeal, surpassing all his people in liberality, and so setting them a princely example. <div eID="gen21487" type="x-p"/>
entries.92d4ad2e948715b1a9cd332124b5dbab18854231: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11894"/><div sID="gen21488" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11894"/>16-18. The prince's possession is to be inalienable, and any portion given to a servant is to revert to his sons at the year of jubilee, that he may have no temptation to spoil his people of their inheritance, as formerly (compare Ahab and Naboth, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.1-1Kgs.21.29">1Ki 21:1-29</reference>). The mention of the year of jubilee implies that there is something literal meant, besides the spiritual sense. The jubilee year was restored after the captivity [Josephus, Antiquities, 14.10,6; 1 Maccabees 6:49]. Perhaps it will be restored under Messiah's coming reign. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.61.2">Is 61:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">3</reference>, where "the acceptable year of the Lord" is closely connected with the comforting of the mourners in Zion, and "the day of vengeance" on Zion's foes. The mention of the prince's sons is another argument against Messiah being meant by "the prince." <div eID="gen21488" type="x-p"/>
entries.672ed65e766896803137d3601e113e603c4e34b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11895"/><div sID="gen21489" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11895"/>19-24. Due regard is to be had for the sanctity of the officiating priests' food, by cooking courts being provided close to their chambers. One set of apartments for cooking was to be at the corners of the inner court, reserved for the flesh of the sin offerings, to be eaten only by the priests whose perquisite it was (<reference osisRef="Lev.6.25">Le 6:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.7.7">7:7</reference>), before coming forth to mingle again with the people; another set at the corners of the outer court, for cooking the flesh of the peace offerings, of which the people partook along with the priests. All this implies that no longer are the common and unclean to be confounded with the sacred and divine, but that in even the least things, as eating and drinking, the glory of God is to be the aim (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.31">1Co 10:31</reference>). <div eID="gen21489" type="x-p"/>

entries.5795f69fce4f0d059c00a5da3ea468fed96f2e65: <div eID="gen32594" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32595" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32596" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32596" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32595" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32597" type="x-p"/> Ordinances of worship prescribed for the prince and for the people, <reference osisRef="Eze.46.1-Eze.46.15">Eze 46:1-15</reference>; and the gifts he may bestow on his sons and servants, <reference osisRef="Eze.46.16-Eze.46.18">Eze 46:16-18</reference>. A description of the courts appointed for boiling or baking any part of the holy oblations, <reference osisRef="Eze.46.19-Eze.46.24">Eze 46:19-24</reference>.
entries.6dcdc13b6bb941761c7b8ef29e32761896192a31: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen32597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32598" type="x-p"/> The burnt-offerings that the prince shall offer - The chief magistrate was always obliged to attend the public worship of God, as well as the priest, to show that the civil and ecclesiastical states were both under the same government of the Lord; and that no one was capable of being prince or priest, who did not acknowledge God in all his ways. It is no wonder that those lands mourn, where neither the established priest nor the civil magistrate either fear or love God. Ungodly priests and profligate magistrates are a curse to any land. In no country have I found both so exemplary for uprightness, as in Britain.
entries.d1db456da3de019ecf16b61603be930fea1ead1a: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen32598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32599" type="x-p"/> According as his hand shall attain unto - According to his ability, to what the providence of God has put in his hand, i.e., his power. This proportion of offerings is different from that prescribed by the Mosaic law, <reference osisRef="Num.15.4-Num.15.12">Num 15:4-12</reference>.
entries.578a4718b07b0b14c06b055dfad373cbbc313d9f: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen32599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32600" type="x-p"/> He that entereth in by the way of the north, etc. - As the north and the south gates were opposite to each other, he that came in at the north must go out at the south; he that came in at the south must go out at the north. No person was to come in at the east gate, because there was no gate at the west; and the people were not permitted to turn round and go out at the same place by which they came in; for this was like turning their backs on God, and the decorum and reverence with which public worship was to be conducted would not admit of this. Besides, returning by the same way must have occasioned a great deal of confusion, where so many people must have jostled each other, in their meetings in different parts of this space.
entries.b99de90754cdf2353f064b9661e17833652ab2f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen32600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32601" type="x-p"/> And the prince in the midst of them - Even he shall act in the same way: he must also go straight forward, and never turn his back to go out at the same gate by which he entered. The prince and the people were to begin and end their worship at the same time.
entries.7e339c927bd52a941e8a302ae48dce04590f37ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen32601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32602" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt prepare it every morning - The evening offering is entirely omitted, which makes an important difference between this and the old laws. See Exodus 29:31-46.
entries.911584417a8f4b48863f19dab3349b1a4358282e: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen32602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32603" type="x-p"/> To the year of liberty - That is, to the year of jubilee, called the year of liberty, because there was then a general release. All servants had their liberty, and all alienated estates returned to their former owners.
entries.562f36b832ceb005ab229c04dadda5e5a258a6b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen32603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32604" type="x-p"/> He brought me thorough the entry - The prophet had entered by the north gate of the court of the priests, where he had seen, a little before, the glory of the Lord, and where he had received all those directions from <reference osisRef="Eze.44.4">Eze 44:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.44.5">Eze 44:5</reference>, to this chapter. From that gate, (see plan Q.) he entered the vestibule by a gate which was by the side of the apartments of the priests, which were along this aisle, (see S.) to the right of the vestibule towards the west. At the extremity of a row of chambers, he remarked, at the west, the place where they boiled the flesh of the sin-offerings, (see T.) They did not boil there the flesh of all sorts of victims, there were other kitchens appointed for that, (see PP): but that only which could not be eaten but in the outer court, and by the priests which were sanctified; such were the parts of the offerings for sins of commission and ignorance, and the offerings of flour with which they were accompanied.
entries.e3119d4af9021b226a55aefb9f1512e640aa91f3: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen32604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32605" type="x-p"/> The trespass-offering - Part of this, and of the sin-offering, and the flour-offering was the portion of the priests. See <reference osisRef="Num.18.9">Num 18:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.18.10">Num 18:10</reference>.
entries.786d78fff8011137a55094ee6e38ca99740c848b: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen32605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32606" type="x-p"/> It was made with boiling places - These were uncovered apartments, where they kept fires for dressing those parts of the peace-offerings, which were made in the temple by individuals through a principle of devotion. On these their families and their friends feasted; and portions were sent to the poor, the widows, and the orphans. And thus the spirit of devotion was the means of preserving the spirit of mercy, charity, and benevolence in the land. How true is that word, "Godliness is profitable for all things."  <chapter eID="Ezek.46"/> <div eID="gen32606" type="x-p"/>

entries.4a8b8ca3b5152fa72d845b0e8dfe6947cb58c0ba: <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.1-Ezek.46.7">Eze 46:1-7</reference> <div eID="gen15346" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Sacrifices for the Sabbath and New Moon</title> <div sID="gen15347" type="x-p"/> As, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.17">Eze 45:17</reference>, it devolved upon the prince to provide and bring the sacrifices for himself and the house of Israel; after the appointment of the sacrifices to be offered at the yearly feasts (<reference osisRef="Ezek.45.18-Ezek.45.25">Eze 45:18-25</reference>), and before the regulation of the sacrifices for the Sabbath and new moon (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.4-Ezek.46.7">Eze 46:4-7</reference>), directions are given as to the conduct of the prince at the offering of these sacrifices (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.1-Ezek.46.3">Eze 46:1-3</reference>). For although the slaughtering and preparation of the sacrifices for the altar devolved upon the priests, the prince was to be present at the offering of the sacrifices to be provided by him, whereas the people were under no obligation to appear before the Lord in the temple except at the yearly feasts. <div eID="gen15347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15348" type="x-p"/> Eze 46:1. <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, The gate of the inner court, which looks toward the east, shall be shut the six working days, and on the Sabbath it shall be opened, and on the day of the new moon it shall be opened.</hi> Eze 46:2. <hi type="italic">And the prince shall come by the way to the porch of the gate from without, and stand at the posts of the gate, and the priests shall prepare his burnt-offering and his peace-offerings, and he shall worship on the threshold of the gate and then go out; but the gate shall not be shut till the evening.</hi> Eze 46:3. <hi type="italic">And the people of the land shall worship at the entrance of that gate on the Sabbaths and on the new moons before Jehovah.</hi> Eze 46:4. <hi type="italic">And the burnt-offering which the prince shall offer to Jehovah shall consist on the Sabbath-day of six lambs without blemish and a ram without blemish;</hi> Eze 46:5. <hi type="italic">And as a meat-offering, an ephah for the ram, and for the lambs as a meat-offering that which his hand may give, and of oil a hin to the ephah (of meal).</hi> Eze 46:6. <hi type="italic">And on the day of the new moon there shall be an bullock, a young ox without blemish, and six lambs and a ram without blemish;</hi> Eze 46:7. <hi type="italic">And he shall put an ephah for the bullock, and an ephah for the ram for the meat-offering, and for the lambs as much as his hand affords, and of oil a hin for the ephah.</hi> - <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.1-Ezek.46.3">Eze 46:1-3</reference> supply and explain the instructions given in <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.1-Ezek.44.3">Eze 44:1-3</reference> concerning the outer eastern gate. As the east gate of the outer court (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.1">Eze 44:1</reference>), so also the east gate of the inner court was to remain closed during the six working days, and only to be opened on the Sabbaths and new moons, when it was to remain open till the evening. The prince was to enter this inner east gate, and to stand there and worship upon the threshold while his sacrifice was being prepared and offered. בּוא דּרך אוּלם is to be taken as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.44.3">Eze 44:3</reference>; but מחוּץ, which is appended, is not to be referred to the entrance into the inner court, as the statement would be quite superfluous so far as this is concerned, since any one who was not already in the inner court must enter the gate-building of the inner court from without, or from the outer court. The meaning of מחוּץ is rather that the prince was to enter, or to go to, the gate porch of the inner court through the outer east gate. There he was to stand at the posts of the gate and worship on the threshold of the gate during the sacrificial ceremony; and when this was over he was to go out again, namely, by the same way by which he entered (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.3">Eze 44:3</reference>). But the people who came to the temple on the Sabbaths and new moons were to worship פּתח, i.e., at the entrance of this gate, outside the threshold of the gate. Kliefoth in wrong in taking פּתח in the sense of through the doorway, as signifying that the people were to remain in front of the outer east gate, and to worship looking at the temple through this gate and through the open gate between. For השּׁער ההוּא roF ., <hi type="italic">hits</hi> gate, can only be the gate of the inner court, which has been already mentioned. There is no force in the consideration which has led Kliefoth to overlook ההוּא, and think of the outer gate, namely, that “it would be unnatural to suppose that the people were to come into the outer court through the outer north and south gates, whilst the outer east gate remained shut (or perhaps more correctly, was opened for the prince), and so stand in front of the inner court,” as it is impossible to see what there is that is unnatural in such a supposition. On the other hand, it is unnatural to assume that the people, who, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.9">Eze 46:9</reference>, were to come through the north and south gates into the outer court at all the מועדים to appear before Jehovah, were not allowed to enter the court upon the Sabbaths and new moons if they should wish to worship before Jehovah upon these days also, but were to stand outside before the gate of the outer court. The difference between the princes and the people, with regard to visiting the temple upon the Sabbaths and new moons, consisted chiefly in this, that the prince could enter by the outer east gate and proceed as far as the posts of the middle gate, and there worship upon the threshold of the gate, whereas the people were only allowed to come into the outer court through the outer north and south gates, and could only proceed to the front of the middle gate. - Eze 46:4. The burnt-offering for the Sabbath is considerably increased when compared with that appointed in the Mosaic law. The law requires two yearling lambs with the corresponding meat-offering (Num 28:9); Ezekiel, six lambs and one ram, and in addition to these a meat-offering for the ram according to the proportion already laid down in <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.24">Eze 45:24</reference> for the festal sacrifices; and for the lambs, מתּת ידו, a gift, a present of his hand, - that is to say, not a handful of meal, but, according to the formula used in alternation with it in <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.7">Eze 46:7</reference>, as much as his hand can afford. For כּאשׁר , see <reference osisRef="Lev.14.30">Lev 14:30</reference>; Lev 25:26. - It is different with the sacrifices of the new moon in <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.6">Eze 46:6</reference> and Eze 46:7. The law of Moses prescribed two bullocks, one ram, and seven lambs, with the corresponding meat-offering, and a he-goat for a sin-offering (Num 28:11-15); the <hi type="italic">thorah</hi> of Ezekiel, on the contrary, omits the sin-offering, and reduces the burnt-offering to one bullock, one ram, and six lambs, together with a meat-offering, according to the proportion already mentioned, which is peculiar to his law. The first תּמימים in <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.6">Eze 46:6</reference> is a copyist’s error for תּמים.
entries.cb3e94b59335ae688512f18749f6f709efe091f8: <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.8-Ezek.46.12">Eze 46:8-12</reference> <div eID="gen15348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15349" type="x-p"/> On the Opening of the Temple for the People, and for the Voluntary Offerings of the Prince. - Eze 46:8. <hi type="italic">And when the prince cometh, he shall go in by the way to the porch of the gate, and by its way shall he go out.</hi> Eze 46:9. <hi type="italic">And when the people of the land come before Jehovah on the feast days, he who enters through the north gate to worship shall go out through the south gate; and he who enters through the south gate shall go out through the north gate: they shall not return through the gate through which they entered, but go out straight forward.</hi> Eze 46:10. <hi type="italic">And the prince shall enter in the midst of them, when they enter; and when they go out, they shall go out (together).</hi> Eze 46:11. <hi type="italic">And at the feast days and holy days the meat-offering shall be an ephah for the bullock, an ephah for the ram, and for the lambs what his hand may give, and of oil a hin for the ephah.</hi> Eze 46:12. <hi type="italic">And when the prince prepares a voluntary burnt-offering or voluntary peace-offerings to Jehovah, they shall open the gate that looks to the east, and he shall prepare his burnt-offerings and his peace-offering as he does on the Sabbath day; and when he has gone out they shall shut the gate after his going out.</hi> - The coming of the people to worship before Jehovah has been already mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.3">Eze 46:3</reference>, but only causally, with reference to the position which they were to take behind the prince in case any individuals should come on the Sabbaths or new moons, on which they were not bound to appear. At the high festivals, on the other hand, every one was to come (<reference osisRef="Deut.16.16">Deu 16:16</reference>); and for this there follow the necessary directions in <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.9">Eze 46:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.10">Eze 46:10</reference>, to prevent crowding and confusion. For the purpose of linking these directions to what comes before, the rule already laid down in <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.2">Eze 46:2</reference> concerning the entrance and exit of the prince is repeated in Eze 46:8. מועדים is supposed by the commentators to refer to the high festivals of the first and seventh months (<reference osisRef="Ezek.45.21">Eze 45:21</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.25">Eze 45:25</reference>); but מועדים does not apply to the same feasts as those which are called הגּים in <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.11">Eze 46:11</reference>, as we may see from the combination of הגּים and מועדים. הגּים is the term applied to the greater annual feasts, as distinguished from the Sabbaths, new moons, and the day of atonement. The מועדים, on the contrary, are all the times and days sanctified to the Lord, including even the Sabbath (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Lev.23.2">Lev 23:2</reference>). It is in this sense that מועדים is used here in <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.9">Eze 46:9</reference>, and not הגּים, because what is laid down concerning the entrance and exit of the people, when visiting the temple, is not merely intended to apply to the high festivals, on which the people were bound to appear before Jehovah, but also to such feast days as the Sabbaths and new moons, whenever individuals from among the people were desirous of their own free-will to worship before the Lord. The latter cases were not to be excluded, although, as <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.10">Eze 46:10</reference> clearly shows, the great feasts were principally kept in mind. For the entrance and exit of the prince in the midst of the people (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.10">Eze 46:10</reference>) apply to the great yearly feasts alone. The <hi type="italic">Chetib</hi> yeetsee'uw יצאוּ in <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.9">Eze 46:9</reference> is to be preferred to the easier <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> יצא, and is not merely the more difficult reading, but the more correct reading also, as two kinds of people are mentioned, - those who entered by the north gate and those who entered by the south. Both are to go out walking straight forward; and neither of them is to turn in the court for the purpose of going out by the gate through which he entered. Even in <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.10">Eze 46:10</reference> יצאוּ is not to be altered, as Hitzig supposes, but to be taken as referring to the prince and the people. - In <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.11">Eze 46:11</reference>, the instructions given in <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.24">Eze 45:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.5">Eze 46:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.7">Eze 46:7</reference>, concerning the quantities composing the meat-offering for the different feasts, are repeated here as rules applicable to all festal times. בּהגּים וּבמועדים has been correctly explained as follows: “at the feasts, and generally at all regular (more correctly, established) seasons,” cf. Eze 45:17. Only the daily sacrifices are excepted from this rule, other regulations being laid down for them in Eze 46:14. - Eze 46:12. The freewill-offerings could be presented on any week-day. And the rules laid down in <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.1">Eze 46:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.2">Eze 46:2</reference> for the Sabbath-offerings of the prince are extended to cases of this kind, with one modification, namely, that the east gate, which had been opened for the occasion, should be closed again as soon as the sacrificial ceremony was over, and not left open till the evening, as on the Sabbath and new moon. נדבה is a substantive: the freewill-offering, which could be either a burnt-offering or a peace-offering.
entries.791d4822ce81936a702e54a03801ff1d5f71c28f: <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.13-Ezek.46.15">Eze 46:13-15</reference> <div eID="gen15349" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Daily Sacrifice</title> <div sID="gen15350" type="x-p"/> Eze 46:13. <hi type="italic">And a yearling lamb without blemish shalt thou prepare as a burnt-offering daily for Jehovah: every morning shalt thou prepare it.</hi> Eze 46:14. <hi type="italic">And a meat-offering shalt thou add to it every morning, a sixth of an ephah, and oil a third of a hin, to moisten the wheaten flour, as a meat-offering for Jehovah: let these be everlasting statutes, perpetually enduring.</hi> Eze 46:15. <hi type="italic">And prepare the lamb, and the meat-offering, and the oil, every morning as a perpetual burnt-offering.</hi> - The preparation of the daily sacrifice is not imposed upon the prince, in harmony with <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.17">Eze 45:17</reference>; it is the duty of the congregation, which the priests have to superintend. Every morning a yearling lamb is to be brought as a burnt-offering. The Mosaic law required such a lamb both morning and evening (Num 28:3-4). The new <hi type="italic">thorah</hi> omits the evening sacrifice, but increases the meat-offering to the sixth of an ephah of meal and the third of a hin of oil, against the tenth of an ephah of meal and the fourth of a hin of oil prescribed by the Mosaic law (Num 28:5). רס, from רסס, ἁπ. λεγ.., to moisten (cf. רסיסים, Sol 5:2). The plural חקּות refers to the burnt-offering and meat-offering. תּמיד is added to give greater force, and, according to the correct remark of Hitzig, appears to be intended as a substitute for לדורתיכם in <reference osisRef="Lev.23.14">Lev 23:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.21">Lev 23:21</reference>, Lev 23:31. The repeated emphasizing of בּבּקר בּבּק shows that the silence as to the evening sacrifice is not a mere oversight of the matter, but that in the new order of worship the evening sacrifice is to be omitted. The <hi type="italic">Chetib</hi> ועשׂוּ is to be retained, in opposition to the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> יעשׂוּ. <div eID="gen15350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15351" type="x-p"/> This brings to an end the new order of worship. The verses which follow in the chapter before us introduce two supplementary notices, - namely, a regulation pointing back to <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.7-Ezek.45.9">Eze 45:7-9</reference>, concerning the right of the prince to hand down or give away his landed property (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.16-Ezek.46.18">Eze 46:16-18</reference>); and a brief description of the sacrificial kitchens for priests and people (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.19-Ezek.46.24">Eze 46:19-24</reference>).
entries.34d16ff16a3e7e6cd7098a072413316592285322: <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.16-Ezek.46.18">Eze 46:16-18</reference> <div eID="gen15351" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">On the Right of the Prince to Dispose of his Landed Property</title> <div sID="gen15352" type="x-p"/> Eze 46:16. <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord Jehovah, If the prince gives a present to one of his sons, it is his inheritance, shall belong to his sons; it is their possession, in an hereditary way.</hi> Eze 46:17. <hi type="italic">But if he gives a present from his inheritance to one of his servants, it shall belong to him till the year of liberty, and then return to the prince; to his sons alone shall his inheritance remain.</hi> Eze 46:18. <hi type="italic">And the prince shall not take from the inheritance of the people, so as to thrust them out of their possession; from his own possession he shall transmit to his sons, that no one of my people be scattered from his possession.</hi> - According to <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.7-Ezek.45.8">Eze 45:7-8</reference>, at the future division of the land among the tribes, a possession was to be given to the prince on both sides of the holy heave and of the city domain, that he might not seize upon a possession by force, as the former princes had done. The prince might give away portions of this royal property, but only within such limits that the design with which a regal possession had been granted might not be frustrated. To his sons, as his heirs, he might make gifts therefrom, which would remain their own property; but if he presented to any one of his servants a portion of his hereditary property, it was to revert to the prince in the year of liberty; just as, according to the Mosaic law, the hereditary field of an Israelite, which had been alienated, was to revert to its hereditary owner (<reference osisRef="Lev.27.24">Lev 27:24</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Lev.25.10-Lev.25.13">Lev 25:10-13</reference>). The suffix in נחלתו (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.16">Eze 46:16</reference>) is not to be taken as referring to the prince, and connected with the preceding words in opposition to the accents, but refers to אישׁ מבּניו. What the prince gives to one of his sons from his landed property shall be his נחלה, i.e., after the manner of an hereditary possession. On the other hand, what the prince presents to one of his servants shall not become hereditary in his case, but shall revert to the prince in the year of liberty, or the year of jubilee. The second half of <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.17">Eze 46:17</reference> reads verbally thus: “only his inheritance is it; as for his sons, it shall belong to them.” - And as the prince was not to break up his regal possession by presents made to servants, so was he (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.18">Eze 46:18</reference>) also not to put any one out of his possession by force, for the purpose, say, of procuring property for his own sons; but was to give his sons their inheritance from his own property alone. For הונה, compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.8">Eze 45:8</reference>, and such passages as <reference osisRef="1Sam.8.14">1Sa 8:14</reference>; 1Sa 22:7. We shall return by and by to the question, how this regulation stands related to the view that the prince is the Messiah.
entries.fecf9356c7cbd982f9d27822d97466df48cec657: <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.19-Ezek.46.24">Eze 46:19-24</reference> <div eID="gen15352" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sacrificial Kitchens for the Priests and for the People</title> <div sID="gen15353" type="x-p"/> Eze 46:19. <hi type="italic">And he brought me up the entrance by the shoulder of the gate to the holy cells for the priests, which looked to the north; and behold there was a place on the outermost side toward the west.</hi> Eze 46:20. <hi type="italic">And he said to me, This is the place where the priests boil the trespass-offering and the sin-offering, where they bake the meat-offering that they may not need to carry it out into the outer court, to sanctify the people.</hi> Eze 46:21. <hi type="italic">And he led me out into the outer court, and caused me to pass by the four corners of the court; and behold, in every corner of the court there was again a court.</hi> Eze 46:22. <hi type="italic">In the four corners of the court were closed courts of forty cubits in length and thirty cubits in breadth; all four corner spaces had one measure.</hi> Eze 46:23. <hi type="italic">And a row of stands was round about therein in all four, and boiling hearths were under the  rows made round about.</hi> Eze 46:24. <hi type="italic">And he said to me, These are the kitchen-house, where the servants of the house boil the slain-offering of the people.</hi> - In the list and description of the subordinate buildings of the temple, the sacrificial kitchens are passed over; and they are therefore referred to here again in a supplementary manner. Ewald has shifted <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.19-Ezek.46.24">Eze 46:19-24</reference>, and placed them after <reference osisRef="Ezek.42.14">Eze 42:14</reference>, which would certainly have been the most suitable place for mentioning the sacrificial kitchens for the priests. But it is evident that they stood here originally, and not there; not only from the fact that in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.46.19">Eze 46:19</reference></hi> the passage to the holy cells (Eze 42:1.) is circumstantially described, which would have been unnecessary if the description of the kitchens had originally followed immediately after <reference osisRef="Ezek.42.14">Eze 42:14</reference>, as Ezekiel was then standing by the cells; but also, and still more clearly, from the words that serve as an introduction to what follows, “he led me back to the door of the house” (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1">Eze 47:1</reference>), which are unintelligible unless he had changed his standing-place between <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.18">Eze 46:18</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1">Eze 47:1</reference>, as is related in <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.19">Eze 46:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.21">Eze 46:21</reference>, since Ezekiel had received the sacrificial <hi type="italic">thorah</hi> (Ezekiel 44:5-46:18) in front of the house (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.4">Eze 44:4</reference>). If <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.19-Ezek.46.24">Eze 46:19-24</reference> had originally stood elsewhere, so that <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1">Eze 47:1</reference> was immediately connected with <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.18">Eze 46:18</reference>, the transition-formula in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1">Eze 47:1</reference></hi> would necessarily have read very differently. - But with this section the right of the preceding one, <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.16-Ezek.46.18">Eze 46:16-18</reference>, which Ewald has arbitrarily interpolated in Ezekiel 45 between <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.8">Eze 45:8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.45.9">Eze 45:9</reference>, to hold its present place in the chapter before us as an appendix, is fully vindicated. - The holy cells (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.19">Eze 46:19</reference>) are those of the northern cell-building (<reference osisRef="Ezek.42.1-Ezek.42.10">Eze 42:1-10</reference>) described in <reference osisRef="Ezek.42.1-Ezek.42.14">Eze 42:1-14</reference> (see Plate I <hi type="italic">L</hi>). בּמּבוא is the approach or way mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ezek.42.9">Eze 42:9</reference>, which led from the northern inner gate to these cells (see Plate I <hi type="italic">l</hi>); not the place to which Ezekiel was brought (Kliefoth), but the passage along which he was led. The spot to which he was conducted follows in אל  (the article before the construct state, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.21">Eze 43:21</reference>, etc.). אל הכּהנים is appended to this in the form of an apposition; and here לשׁכות is to be repeated in thought: to those for the priests. 'הפּנות צ belongs to הלשׁכות. There, i.e., by the cells, was a space set apart at the outermost (hindermost) sides toward the west (Plate I <hi type="italic">M</hi>), for the boiling of the flesh of the trespass-offering and sin-offering, and the baking of the <hi type="italic">minchah</hi>, - that is to say, of those portions of the sacrifices which the priests were to eat in their official capacity (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Ezek.42.13">Eze 42:13</reference>). For the motive assigned in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.46.20">Eze 46:20</reference></hi> for the provision of special kitchens for this object, see the exposition of Eze 44:19. <div eID="gen15353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15354" type="x-p"/> In addition to these, kitchens were required for the preparation of the sacrificial meals, which were connected with the offering of the <hi type="italic">shelamim</hi>, and were held by those who presented them. These sacrificial kitchens for the people are treated of in <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.20">Eze 46:20</reference>-24. They were situated in the four corners of the outer court (Plate I N). To show them to the prophet, the angel leads him into the outer court. The holy cells (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.19">Eze 46:19</reference>) and the sacrificial kitchens for the priests (<reference osisRef="Ezek.46.20">Eze 46:20</reference>) were also situated by the outside wall of the inner court; and for this reason Ezekiel had already been led out of the inner court, where he had received the sacrificial <hi type="italic">thorah</hi>, through the northern gate of the court by the way which led to the holy cells, that he might be shown the sacrificial kitchens. When, therefore, it is stated in <reference osisRef="Ezek.46.21">Eze 46:21</reference> that “he led me out into the outer court,” יוציאני can only be explained on the supposition that the space from the surrounding wall of the inner court to the way which led from the gate porch of that court to the holy cells, and to the passage which continued this way in front of the cells (Plate I <hi type="italic">l</hi> and <hi type="italic">m</hi>), was regarded as an appurtenance of the inner court. In every one of the four corners of the outer court there was a (small) courtyard in the court. The repetition of 'חצר בּמקצע הח has a distributive force. The small courtyards in the four corners of the court were קטרות, i.e., not “uncovered,” as this would be unmeaning, since all courts or courtyards were uncovered; nor “contracted” (Böttcher), for קטר has no such meaning; nor “<hi type="italic">fumum exhalantia</hi>,” as the Talmudists suppose; nor “bridged over” (Hitzig), which there is also nothing in the language to sustain; but in all probability <hi type="italic">atria clausa</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">muris cincta et janius clausa</hi> (Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>.), from קטר; in Aram. <hi type="italic">ligavit</hi>; in Ethiop. <hi type="italic">clausit, obseravit januam</hi>. The word מהקצעות is marked with <hi type="italic">puncta extraordinaria</hi> by the Masoretes as a suspicious word, and is also omitted in the Septuagint and Vulgate. Böttcher and Hitzig have therefore expunged it as a gloss. But even Hitzig admits that this does not explain how it found its way into the text. The word is a <hi type="italic">Hophal</hi> participle of קצע, in the sense of cornered off, cut off into corners, and is in apposition to the suffix to לארבּעתּם, - literally, one measure wax to all four, the spaces or courtyards cut off in the corners. For this appositional use of the participle, compare 1Ki 14:6. There is also a difference of opinion as to the meaning of the word טוּר, which only occurs here and in Exo 28:17. and <reference osisRef="Ezek.39.10">Eze 39:10</reference>, where it signifies “row,” and not “enclosure” (Kliefoth). טירות, which follows, is evidently merely the feminine plural, from טוּר, as טירה is also derived from טוּר, in the sense of “to encircle” (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Ps.69.26">Psa 69:26</reference>). Consequently טוּר does not mean a covering or boundary wall, but a row or shelf of brickwork which had several separate shelves, under which the cooking hearths were placed. מבשּׁלות, not kitchens, but cooking hearths; strictly speaking a <hi type="italic">partic. Piel</hi>, things which cause to boil. -  בּית המּבשּׁלים  - .liob ot e, kitchen house. משׁרתּי הבּית, the temple servants, as distinguished from the servants of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.15-Ezek.44.16">Eze 44:15-16</reference>), are the Levites (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.11-Ezek.44.12">Eze 44:11-12</reference>). עשׂוּי is construed as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.17">Eze 40:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.41.18">Eze 41:18</reference>-19.  <chapter eID="Ezek.46"/> <div eID="gen15354" type="x-p"/>

               <ns0:p n="1">1 THus saith the Lord GOD; the gate <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">'Twas the East-gate of the Court next to the Temple, or which did lead into the inmost Court, where the Altar of burnt-offering stood.</ns0:note> of the inward court that looketh to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward the east shall be shut <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This explains that of <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 44.2. <ns0:hi>let.</ns0:hi> d. f. g.</ns0:note> the six working dayes <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Or every day that is a working day.</ns0:note>; but on the sabbath <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">On that holy rest the prospect into the Temple, and to the Altar shall be free.</ns0:note> it shall be opened <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The Priests should open it.</ns0:note>, and in the day of the new moon <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This one festival is named, but all the rest are included, this gate was to be shut onely on working dayes, therefore to be open on all holy dayes, which were dayes of holy Service to God.</ns0:note> it shall be opened.</ns0:p>
